claims.text: A V–Cr–Ti–W refractory HEA will exhibit low neutron activation under fusion-reactor plasma-facing conditions.
A V–Cr–Ti–W refractory HEA will exhibit superior high-temperature mechanical properties under fusion-reactor plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed bulk alloy has a near-equiatomic V, Cr, Ti, and W composition.
The proposed initial material is as-cast and annealed.
The proposed V–Cr–Ti–W alloy forms a stable single-phase microstructure, potentially BCC.
The proposed alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Plasma-facing component operating environments can involve temperatures above 1200°C, high heat flux, and neutron-rich irradiation.
The intrinsic high-entropy effect stabilizes the single-phase refractory structure.
Stabilization by the high-entropy effect minimizes radiation-induced elemental segregation.
Stabilization by the high-entropy effect minimizes irradiation-induced phase decomposition.
V, Cr, Ti, and W provide refractory, high-melting-point characteristics.
V, Cr, Ti, and W have low neutron-activation profiles.
The activation products of V, Cr, Ti, and W generally consist of short-lived radioisotopes.
Combining refractory characteristics with low activation will retain mechanical strength under irradiation.
Combining refractory characteristics with low activation will minimize long-lived radioactive waste.
The V–Cr–Ti–W HEA is expected to retain high-temperature mechanical integrity under simulated fusion-reactor conditions.
The V–Cr–Ti–W HEA is expected to accumulate fewer long-lived radioactive isotopes than conventional low-activation ferritic/martensitic steels.
EUROFER97 and related low-activation steels suffer reduced mechanical performance at the extreme temperatures experienced by plasma-facing components.
The optimum V–Cr–Ti–W composition has not been established.
The long-term irradiation behavior of the V–Cr–Ti–W HEA under realistic fusion conditions requires experimental validation.
